Cyber Attack Disrupts Zimbabwe’s Automotive Industry Operations

A cyber attack targeting Zimbabwe’s automotive industry has forced several firms to halt production and suspend IT-dependent operations, with industry sources confirming that the incident is ongoing and its full impact yet to be determined.

The attack, which began early Monday morning, has so far affected at least four major automotive manufacturers and component assembly plants operating in the Harare and Bulawayo industrial zones. According to a statement released by the Zimbabwe Automotive Manufacturers Association (ZAMA), initial indications point to a ransomware infection that has compromised internal networks and rendered key software systems inoperable.

“Production lines at multiple sites have been brought to a standstill as a precautionary measure, pending a thorough investigation and restoration of secure systems,” said ZAMA secretary-general Tawanda Nyathi. “We are working closely with cybersecurity experts and relevant authorities to contain the breach and resume normal operations as soon as possible.”

Employees at affected sites reported being sent home or reassigned to manual tasks as digital scheduling, inventory, and quality control platforms remained locked. One worker at the Motec Assembly Plant in Harare, who asked not to be named, described the scene: “Management told us to stop all work involving computers. We’re waiting for updates, but most of the plant is quiet. People are worried about their shifts and wages.”

Estimates provided by ZAMA suggest that as many as 3,000 workers across the sector may be idled or placed on reduced hours. “We are engaging with unions and labor representatives to address concerns around pay and job security during this disruption,” Nyathi said.

Analysts caution that the timing of the attack compounds existing challenges facing Zimbabwe’s automotive sector, which has struggled with supply chain delays and rising input costs in recent months. “The industry is already under pressure to modernize its infrastructure and boost output, so a prolonged shutdown could further erode confidence and delay recovery,” noted independent industry analyst Rutendo Chikowore.

While the exact financial toll of the attack remains unclear, automotive firms have acknowledged that the inability to process orders, manage inventories, or complete scheduled deliveries is likely to result in significant revenue losses. “The longer the systems remain offline, the more difficult it will be for manufacturers to meet customer demand and maintain cash flow,” Chikowore added.

As of Tuesday afternoon, no group has claimed responsibility for the cyber attack. ZAMA has urged all member firms to review their cyber defenses and implement emergency protocols. The industry association is expected to provide a further update once the extent of the disruption and a timeline for system restoration become clearer.
